title: The same customer gets two emails
concept: Objects that compare equal must have equal hashes
symptom: Ada is on the newsletter as Ada@Example.com and on the promo list as ada@example.com. The mailer treats her as two people and sends two emails, and the directory registers her twice, even though customers == customers says they are equal.
failingTest:
import unittest

from customer import Customer
from directory import Directory
from mailer import Mailer


class Failing(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_the_same_person_in_two_cases_is_one_recipient(self):
        newsletter = [Customer("Ada@Example.com"), Customer("bob@example.com")]
        promo = [Customer("ada@example.com")]
        mailer = Mailer()
        self.assertEqual(mailer.send_to_all(newsletter, promo, subject="Sale"), 2)

    def test_the_directory_finds_a_customer_whatever_the_case(self):
        directory = Directory()
        self.assertTrue(directory.add(Customer("Ada@Example.com", "Ada")))
        self.assertFalse(directory.add(Customer("ada@example.com")))
        self.assertEqual(len(directory), 1)
        self.assertEqual(directory.find("ADA@EXAMPLE.COM").name, "Ada")
regressionTests:
import unittest

from customer import Customer
from directory import Directory


class Regression(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_different_people_stay_different(self):
        self.assertNotEqual(Customer("ada@example.com"), Customer("bob@example.com"))
        directory = Directory()
        directory.add(Customer("ada@example.com"))
        directory.add(Customer("bob@example.com"))
        self.assertEqual(len(directory), 2)

    def test_the_email_is_kept_as_the_customer_typed_it(self):
        self.assertEqual(Customer("Ada@Example.com").email, "Ada@Example.com")

    def test_the_first_registration_wins(self):
        directory = Directory()
        directory.add(Customer("Ada@Example.com", "Ada"))
        directory.add(Customer("ada@example.com", "Someone else"))
        self.assertEqual(directory.find("ada@example.com").email, "Ada@Example.com")

    def test_unknown_emails_are_not_found(self):
        self.assertIsNone(Directory().find("nobody@example.com"))
rootCause: __eq__ compares emails ignoring case, but __hash__ hashes the email as typed. Equal objects must have equal hashes, so sets and dicts, which look in a bucket chosen by the hash, never even compare Ada@Example.com with ada@example.com. The hash must be computed from the same normalised value that equality uses.

wrongFixes.whyWrong: Lowercasing the email in __init__ makes equality and hashing agree, but it throws away what the customer typed, so every email now goes out and displays in lower case.

grading.question: State the rule that connects __eq__ and __hash__.
grading.ideal: If a == b then hash(a) == hash(b). The converse need not hold.

grading.question: Why did the set not even call __eq__ on the two Adas?
grading.ideal: It first picks a bucket from the hash. Different hashes mean different buckets, so the two objects are never compared.

grading.question: Why is normalising inside __init__ a worse fix than normalising inside __hash__?
grading.ideal: It destroys the original value, which the app may need to show or send as typed.

turns.text: Ada gets two emails because Ada@Example.com and ada@example.com are treated as different customers in a set.
__eq__ ignores case but __hash__ does not, so equal customers land in different hash buckets and a set never compares them. I hash the lower-cased email, matching __eq__, and keep the email as typed.
